summary: Intermittent high P99 latency and client timeouts on customer-dedicated cluster due to cross-tenant GPU memory pressure
description:
Issue summary:
Customer (Atlas AI) reports intermittent spikes in P99 latency for text-generation API when running on their dedicated cluster. Spikes correlate with increased 504/ETIMEDOUT responses from the SDK. Problem appears to be cluster-local (does not affect hosted API).

Impact:
- Approximately 2-4% of requests for Atlas AI experienced >=2s additional latency during spikes, with occasional 504s leading to upstream retries.
- Customer reports user-facing degraded throughput for batch inference jobs and increased error rates on their ingest pipeline.

Environment:
- Dedicated pool: atl-dedicated-1 (us-east-1)
- Nodes: 8x A100-80GB (mixed pod allocations)
- Autoscaler config: target_utilization_cpu=0.7, target_utilization_gpu=0.8, min_replicas=4, max_replicas=12
- Routing policy: region-first, pinned model versions.

Timeline / Observations:
- 2026-03-12 11:05 UTC: First customer slack ping via #support-atlas-ai complaining about timeouts.
- 2026-03-12 11:10 UTC: Support triage, opened ticket, asked for examples and request IDs.
- 2026-03-12 11:15–11:45 UTC: SRE examined Grafana; saw transient increases in GPU memory utilization on 2 nodes and an uptick in kernel preemption events.
- 2026-03-12 11:30 UTC: Noted autoscaler did not add capacity despite rising queue length; pods on 2 nodes showed high OOM peaks in metrics.
- 2026-03-12 12:05 UTC: Applied temporary routing workaround to shift Atlas traffic to warm standby nodes; latency improved immediately for customer.

Steps to reproduce (observed pattern):
1. Run a mix of token-generating small chat workloads and a few heavy-batch requests concurrently on the dedicated pool.
2. Observe intermittent growth in KV cache allocations and per-process GPU memory leading to fragmentation spikes.
3. Serving runtime begins throttling new sessions (head-of-line effects), increasing p99 latency and causing SDK timeouts.

Logs & Metrics (selected):
- Grafana panel: /d/redwood/serving/cluster/atl-dedicated-1 (spike at 2026-03-12T11:20Z)
- node-exporter: /metrics/node123 gpu_memory_total=81920MB gpu_memory_used=79000MB  (sustained for ~60s)
- runtime logs (node123): "Evicting KV cache slice due to GPU memory pressure" repeated 30x in 2m
- autoscaler logs: "scale_decision: no_scale_required" at 11:18 despite queue_length crossing threshold

Hypothesis:
- A tenant running large-batch jobs (unrelated customer or internal test) temporarily consumed disproportionate contiguous GPU memory causing fragmentation and eviction of other processes' KV caches. This created head-of-line blocking where in-flight sessions waited for memory compaction/eviction cycles. Autoscaler mis-evaluated GPU pressure because fragmentation raised used_memory but not scheduler-visible utilization metrics, so it did not scale quickly enough.

Immediate mitigation applied:
- Re-routed Atlas AI traffic to designated warm nodes (manual routing override) at 12:05 UTC — p99 returned to baseline within 90s.
- Placed noisy-neighbor label on the pool and throttled background batch jobs flagged in internal tenant logs.

Planned remediation and follow-up:
- Short term (SRE): add a gating metric to autoscaler that factors contiguous GPU allocation pressure (OOM/eviction counters) and trigger faster scale-up when those counters cross threshold. (Owner: Ethan Carter)
- Mid term (Platform): implement per-tenant soft memory limits and prefer pod placement to avoid co-locating large-batch tenants with latency-sensitive tenants. (Owner: Scheduling team)
- Long term (Product): expose tenant isolation options in Console (dedicated placement profiles) and recommend Atlas AI use reserved warm nodes for peak windows.

Customer-facing note:
- We provided Atlas AI with the temporary routing workaround and a short post-incident summary. Customer requested update on permanent isolation controls and faster autoscale response.
